I haven't told anyone how much Dadaji's shop closing hurt, and it felt like she just knew. Then she said the cards didn't like "a journey west" this year. And, well, the Pune internship is west. I haven't replied to their mail yet. Don't laugh. I know how it sounds. But she was so gentle, and she was right about the hurt, so maybe she's right about Pune too?

passage: Saurabh, my boy, you're asking whether to trust the man at the temple gate. Let your Sonali Bua tell you what happened to me. I was nineteen, the first girl in our family with an engineering seat, in Pune. A week before I was to leave, a face reader stopped me outside the market. He looked at me kindly and said, 'You carry an old hurt you rarely mention.' Beta, I went cold. I thought of my father's shop fire, which I never spoke about. I trusted him at once. Then he said, 'Going far west this year brings loss.' Pune was west. I cried for two days and nearly gave up the seat. My mother finally asked, 'What hurt did he name?' He hadn't named anything. I had filled it in myself. I went to Pune. So by all means listen to him, Saurabh. Just notice what he doesn't say.

qa.q: What did the face reader say about going far west?
qa.a: He said, 'Going far west this year brings loss.'

qa.q: Why did Sonali Bua trust the face reader so quickly?
qa.a: His line about an old hurt made her think of her father's shop fire, so she felt deeply seen and trusted him at once.

qa.q: Which question changed Sonali Bua's decision, and what can Saurabh learn from it?
qa.a: Her mother asked what hurt he had named, and she realised he named nothing; Saurabh can check whether a reader says anything specific before letting it steer him.

qa.q: How might the mother in Sonali Bua's story have felt watching her daughter cry for two days?
qa.a: She was likely worried that a stranger's warm words were about to cost her daughter a hard-won seat, which is why she asked such a careful question.

grounding: An aunt tells her nephew how a reader's warm, general line made her feel seen at nineteen and nearly steered her to give up a college seat.

passage: The Delhi train was six hours late, and Kunal, twenty, sat on his backpack on the cold platform at Jhansi with his phone at eight percent. A man with a notebook and a shawl sat beside him and offered to read his face for free. 'You carry an old hurt you rarely mention,' he said softly. Kunal's throat tightened. He thought of his mother leaving when he was small, something he told no one. The man patted his knee. 'And the partnership you're planning will bring loss.' Kunal stared. He and his friend Samir were about to start a small wedding photography business. How did he know? Kunal used his last battery to text Samir: 'maybe we wait a year. bad feeling.' Samir replied, 'what? since when?' Kunal didn't answer. The man was already talking to the next passenger.

qa.q: Where was Kunal waiting for the delayed train?
qa.a: He sat on his backpack on the cold platform at Jhansi.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when the man mentioned an old hurt?
qa.a: His throat tightened; he felt seen and moved, because he thought of his mother leaving, something he told no one.

qa.q: At what point could Kunal have stopped the reading from steering him, and how?
qa.a: Before texting Samir, he could have asked himself whether the lines were specific at all, and seen the man move to the next passenger with the same routine.

qa.q: How might Samir feel receiving 'maybe we wait a year. bad feeling.'?
qa.a: Samir would likely be confused and hurt, since their plan suddenly changed with no reason Samir could understand.

grounding: A young man stranded on a platform feels seen by a stranger's general line and lets that trust steer him to delay a business plan with his friend.
